In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size. For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like: > An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group. For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like: > A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5. :::

live_data_statements: However, side effects can confound other state measures; especially the longer participants are immersed.
After attaching sensors, subjects were seated and instructed to minimize movements but not be physically tense.
During Experiment 1, participants were immersed for 26 minutes in VR with a Stroop task lasting 5 minutes.
During Experiment 2, participants were immersed for 74 minutes in VR, with four Stroop tasks lasting 20 minutes in total.
Participants were given written and oral instructions simultaneously in French.
Written color, font color, and congruent and incongruent stimuli were randomized to reduce repetition priming while performing the oral Stroop task (Mills et al., 2019).
After the questionnaires, subjects were immersed in a virtual relaxation room to rest.
The subjects were healthy volunteers.

Before participating, subjects were asked to match the following inclusion and exclusion criteria: being aged between 18 and 39 years old; No alcohol for 24h before attending the experiment; No caffeine 12h before the experimental session; No smoking or taking any drugs 12h before the experimental session (Shields et al., 2016); Normal or corrected-to-normal vision; Sufficient sleep 7 to 9 hours as stipulated in (Hirshkowitz et al., 2015); No musculoskeletal, neurological (including epilepsy), or balance disorders.

125 subjects participated in Experiment 1 with a mean age of 25.05 ± 4.73, 62 women, 62 men, and 1 non-binary. 31 subjects participated in Experiment 2 with a mean age of 23.90 ± 3.65, 14 women, 14 men, and 3 non-binaries.

Participants filled out profile surveys before attending the experiment to measure possible profile-based biases between conditions and experiments (Shields et al., 2016; Mittelstaedt, 2020; Shields, 2020; Hertzum, 2021; Howard & Van Zandt, 2021; Jasper et al., 2021; MacArthur et al., 2021; Y. Wang et al., 2021; Widyanti & Hafizhah, 2021; Cao et al., 2022; Harris et al., 2022; da Silva Marinho et al., 2022; Jang et al., 2022; Martingano et al., 2022; Torres et al., 2022; Tian et al., 2022; Maneuvrier et al., 2022).
Participants were mostly university students.

Still, the ECG features were less represented here, probably because participants were instructed to breathe calmly to relax, which impacted their heart behavior, so it would be equivalent to Baseline.
The more participants were immersed, the more they reported those VRISE.
Hence, how long participants are immersed drove different reporting.
In experiment 2, the Dual task and the Stressful conditions were rated similarly stressful, showing that participants were aroused by a cognitively challenging task similar to high noise.
Immersion duration should be chosen, so participants are not impacted by Visual fatigue and Cybersickness, although it didn't seem to impact Cognitive load and Stress reporting.
Participants were exposed to 25 congruent, and 25 incongruent words with the timing presented supplementary materials (file 2).

Consequently, H7 is partially supported as physiological responses differ between Stroop tasks depending on how long participants are immersed, driving different physiological effects independently of specific state induction.
In comparison, our participants were immersed for 74 minutes.

Physiological features were differently associated with each state as ET was more associated with VRISE, although the longer participants were immersed, the more EDA features were associated with VRISE.
Furthermore, suppose subjects are asked to estimate side effects, stress, or high cognitive load at rest, during relaxation, and then during/after stimuli administration.

"states" means Cybersickness, Visual fatigue, Cognitive load, and Acute Stress: -H1: Subjective state (VRSQ, NASA-TLX, STAI-6) differ between experimental conditions implying states are differently perceived depending on state induction -H2: Stroop task performances differ between experimental conditions implying states have different influences on it -H3: Physiological responses differ between experimental conditions implying the 4 Stroop task -hence states inductionstimuli drive different physiological effects -H4: Subjective states (VRSQ, NASA-TLX, STAI-6) depending on which running order (moment in the entire procedure) they are declared after Stroop tasks implying how long participants are immersed drives different reporting -H5: Stroop task performances differ between the running order they fulfill, implying time influences them -H6: Physiological responses differ between steps implying Baseline, Stroop, Relaxation, and Endline drive different physiological effects and that Relaxation or Endline is sufficient for participants' physiological markers to come back to Baseline after state induction -H7: Physiological responses differ between Stroop tasks depending on which order they are performed, implying how long participants are immersed drives different physiological effects independently of specific state induction -H8: Behavioral and physiological features are strongly correlated with each subjective state showing that their variations are linked differently with specific states The general hypothesis is Hgeneral: we can differentiate Cybersickness, Visual fatigue, Cognitive load, and Acute Stress psychophysiological variations in VR.

text.text: Virtual Reality (VR) is increasingly used to study Cognitive load and Acute Stress.
But VR comes with side effects such as Cybersickness and Visual fatigue.
It remains unclear if we can dissociate psychophysiological responses due to confounding effects.
Hence, we conducted two experiments to study and distinguish them.
Participants fulfilled a Baseline, Stroop task under four different experimental conditions, Relaxation and Endline.
We recorded Stroop performances, Eye tracking (ET), Electrocardiography (ECG), Electrodermal activity (EDA), self-reported Cognitive load, Stress, Cybersickness, Visual fatigue, and Disorientation.
Pupil diameter, Blink frequency, Fixations, HR, HRV, and Skin Conductance Response derived between the different conditions.
Most of the extracted features from ET, ECG, and EDA showed no differences between states.

Despite relaxation steps, Saccade ratio, Blink frequency, Blink duration and Pupil size for ET, Heart rate for ECG, Rise time of the mean skin conductance level, the Arc length of the skin conductance level for EDA were still not back equivalent to baseline.
Cognitive load differs from Acute stress based on the Heart rate feature from the ECG sensor.
Cognitive load provoked more response with EDA features than Visual fatigue / Cybersickness with the ALSC feature.
However, most of those differences have small effect sizes.
We underline a 60 minutes immersion "limit."
ET was more sensitive to Visual fatigue / Cybersickness compared to Cognitive load and Acute Stress and ECG to Cognitive load compared to Acute Stress.
We documented physiological features varying depending on the state and which one allowed their differentiation.
However, side effects can confound other state measures; especially the longer participants are immersed.
More experimental inputs are necessary to tackle this research question.

text.text: Finally, to the best of knowledge, there is no evidence that different states (in the rest of the article, when we refer to states, we imply cybersickness, visual fatigue, cognitive load, and acute stress all together to avoid relisting them) can be clearly distinguished based on psychophysiological measures (Maraj et al., 2021; Souchet et al., 2021).

A significant issue of human response to VR is the ability to encompass a variety of complex psychophysiological variations depending on numerous factors (Krohn et al., 2020; Michela et al., 2019).

Finally, considering possible links between states (Souchet et al., 2021; Souchet, Lourdeaux, et al., 2022), it is unclear whether it is possible to differentiate them solely based on psychophysiological signals.

text.text: This paper documents an attempt to distinguish cybersickness, visual fatigue, cognitive load, and acute stress in VR based on behavioral, selfreported (called "subjective" in the rest of the paper), and physiological data (ECG, EDA, ET) acquired in two randomized controlled (between and within-subject) studies with participants recorded at baseline, during a Stroop task a relaxation period, and an Endline (similar to baseline but at the end of the procedure).

We tackle three research questions through height hypotheses to identify specific physiological features associated with each state, the impact of a relaxation period and immersion duration on those features, and which features allow states differentiation.
The paper follows an Introduction, Methods, Results, and Discussion (IMRaD) structure.
Cybersickness has been defined as an uncomfortable side effect experienced by users of immersive interfaces commonly used for VR (Nesbitt & Nalivaiko, 2018, p. 1).

text.text: Gaze movements and blink frequency are the leading features in assessing Cybersickness (four out of eight papers).
In addition to Gaze patterns, pupil diameter, fixations, and saccades are also used.
The studies included M = 31.00 ± 16.44 participants with a M = 25.67 ± 2.03 years old and a M = 16.58 ± 11.97 minutes stimuli duration.
HTC Vive, pro eye, is the most commonly used HMD.
Overall, the results from past work we reviewed indicate that Cybersickness increases over time and is characterized by a blink frequency increase.

The studies included M = 26.40 ± 14.92 participants with a M = 25.11 ± 4.16 years old and a M = 14.89 ± 7.98 minutes stimuli duration.
HTC Vive is the most used HMD.
Overall, the results indicate that HR increases with Cybersickness in VR, and Cybersickness reduction techniques tend to decrease this HR rise in VR.

text.text: Overall, Skin Conductance Response (SCR) is the leading feature used to assess Cybersickness (five out of eight papers) without many details in the exact extracted features from SRC.
The studies included M = 31.38 ± 18.07 participants with a M = 24.17 ± 4.30 years old and a M = 11.86 ± 8.71 minutes stimuli duration.
HTC Vive, and pro are the most used HMDs.
Overall results of those work indicate that SCR features increase in correlation with cybersickness levels.
In summary, the 17 studies we presented, no matter the sensor used, included 27.00 ± 13.62 participants, aged 25.47 ± 3.85, with a stimuli duration of 15.46 ± 9.95 minutes.
The most represented stimuli are roller coasters, flying, and driving, which are obvious choices for studying Cybersickness.
However, no standard stimuli were developed based on previous work.
The main physiological features used to assess Cybersickness are blink frequency, HR, and SCR, which are associated with Cybersickness.
Cybersickness increases with VR exposure duration.

Stress is the individual state of uncertainty about what needs to be done to safeguard physical, mental, or social well-being (Peters et al., 2017).

text.text: Acute Stress is a sudden or short time stressor (trauma, perceived threat, death of a loved one, job loss…) in opposition to chronic Stress (long-time stressor) (Fink, 2007, p. 192-193).

text.text: The Autonomic Nervous System (ANS) adapts the organism to internal and external changes, maintaining bodily homeostasis and coordinating Stress's bodily responses (Richter & Wright, 2013a; Johnson, 2018).
text.formatted: The Autonomic Nervous System (ANS) adapts the organism to internal and external changes, maintaining bodily homeostasis and coordinating Stress's bodily responses <ref type="bibr">(Richter & Wright, 2013a;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b146">Johnson, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: ANS has three subdivisions: -Sympathetic Nervous System (SNS) (Richter & Wright, 2013c) controls the "fight or flight" response preparing the body for physical activity, the effort to either fight off or flee from danger (Chamberlain & Meuret, 2017) -Parasympathetic Nervous System (PNS) (Richter & Wright, 2013b) controls the "rest and digest" response, restoring to counterbalance the stress reaction -Enteric Nervous System (ENS) controls the "gut-brain axis" gastrointestinal function (Rao & Gershon, 2016) Those bodily responses include various physiological variations assessed with ET, ECG, and EDA (Rastgoo et al., 2018; Arza et al., 2019; Armario et al., 2020; McNamara & Mehta, 2020; Nath et al., 2020).

text.text: Overall, SCR and derivate features (mean, sd) are the leading features used to assess acute Stress (twelve out of fifteen papers).
The studies included M = 37.00 ± 29.78 participants with a M = 25.76 ± 4.15 years old and a M = 11.55 ± 6.46 minutes stimuli duration.
HTC Vive, is the most used HMD.
Overall results of those work indicate that SCR and SCL feature increases with Stress in VR.
The 26 studies we presented, no matter the sensor used, included 44.46 ± 35.23 participants, aged 25.71 ± 4.49, with stimuli duration of 12.56 ± 7.81: see supplementary materials (file 1).
Although the Trier Social Stress Test (TSST) -a gold standard in stress studies -and the Stroop task are used, no standard stimuli arise from those previous work.
The physiological features the most represented to assess acute Stress in VR are pupil diameter (decreases), HR (increases), RMSSD (decreases), SCR, and SCL (increases).
In our presentation of previous work measuring Cybersickness, Visual fatigue, Cognitive load, and Acute Stress with ET, ECG, and EDA, we gathered 69 papers.
Overall, those studies included 36.67 ± 29.41 participants who were 26.61 ± 4.74 years old and were presented with stimuli with a duration of 20.05 ± 17.70 minutes.
In the supplementary materials (file 1), we display boxplots comparing the number of participants' mean age and stimuli durations between states.
From one state to another, these numbers can be quite different.
Across these studies, the same physiological signals were recorded, and similar measures, e.g., HRV, were used.
A growing part of the literature uses several sensors (ET + ECG + EDA) to assess these states.
However, only one state is assessed at a time, possibly missing confounds or the effect of other states.
Previous work aims to elicit each state in isolation, and hence, they create stimuli for that purpose.
But this leaves out other plausible co-occurring states with the same stimuli disregarding alternative hypotheses or explanations in physiological variations by focusing the spotlight on one source.
Furthermore, confounding effects are well-documented with studies relying on physiological data (Howards, 2018).
text.formatted: Furthermore, confounding effects are well-documented with studies relying on physiological data <ref type="bibr" target="#b131">(Howards, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: In our case, one psychophysiological state could influence another or better explain physiological variations.
Such confounding effects make it hard to differentiate one state from another.
The various data processing methods for hypothesis testing make findings hard to generalize.

These points are relevant whether data is acquired with ET, ECG, or EDA (Dirican & Göktürk, 2011; Sirois & Brisson, 2014; Shaffer & Ginsberg, 2017; Clay et al., 2019; Hughes et al., 2019; Lohani et al., 2019; Tao et al., 2019; Abdelall et al., 2020; Wulvik et al., 2020; Czerniak et al., 2021; Giorgi et al., 2021).

text.text: Typically, research focusing on Stress and Cognitive load pays little attention to the possible impacts of Cybersickness or Visual fatigue during their physiological data recording.
Conversely, researchers focusing on Cybersickness or Visual fatigue would not consider Stress or Cognitive load induced by tasks during their physiological data recording.
The same issues might apply to Presence (Slater et al., 2022) or other psychological aspects triggered by VR.
In summary, alternative explanations to measured psychophysiological variations are, at best, evoked in previous work within material and methods or discussion and limitation sections.
By extension, contributions regarding human physiological variations under VR exposure often rely on correlations with questionnaire-based data (E. Chang et al., 2020).
text.formatted: By extension, contributions regarding human physiological variations under VR exposure often rely on correlations with questionnaire-based data (E. <ref type="bibr">Chang et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Yet, questionnaires are not all standardized.
Furthermore, questionnaires can be biased (Palaniappan & Kum, 2019).

text.text: In other words, a set of questions can influence participants' self-reporting.
Mentioning Cybersickness and Visual fatigue specifically implies that users are experiencing (and expecting) side effects if they are mentioned at the consent step or assessed before immersion.

Therefore, the complex role of placebo and nocebo effects could even step in, depending on users' traits and emotions relating to the VR experience, as documented in medicine (Faasse et al., 2019; Geers et al., 2020).

text.text: Interestingly, Stroop stimuli also illustrate confusion in psychophysiological effects that are expected to be induced via such tasks, whether Cognitive load related or Stress related.
The Stroop task has not been designed to induce and study Cybersickness or Visual fatigue, which reduces that bias.

Hence, as a well-established and controlled set of stimuli, the Stroop task appears to be a good pick to test hypotheses about Cybersickness, Visual fatigue, Cognitive load, and Acute Stress in VR differentiation.
1.8 Research questions and contributions Previous work show that features extracted from ET, ECG, and EDA allow for measuring Cybersickness, Visual fatigue, Cognitive load, and Stress.
However, discussions in previous work regularly indicate confounding effects that could mitigate the reliability of results.
Possible confounding effects induce artifacts when trying to measure each state independently.
Concretely, physiological variations could be wrongly associated with one state as another could provoke similar variations.
E.g., heart rate in VR increases with Stress and with Cybersickness or with Stress and Cognitive load.
Hence, it is necessary to make sure we can differentiate each state subjectively, behaviorally, and physiologically.
Identifying robust and specific physiological markers for each state is crucial.
Finally, since stimuli are not standardized, relying on long-established psychological tests such as the Stroop task could better isolate each state.

Based on the review of previous work, three main research questions (RQ) arise when trying to measure Cybersickness, Visual fatigue, Cognitive load, and Acute Stress: -RQ1: What are the physiological features characterizing each state? -RQ2: Can we differentiate between different states according to psychophysiological responses? -RQ3: Does using VR to study cognitive load and stress trigger confounding effects in physiological measures due to Cybersickness and Visual fatigue?
Simply put, we aimed to study what we actually measure with ET, ECG, and EDA and with those stimuli.
We conducted two experiments and tested 8 hypotheses to tackle those research questions.

The ECG signal can be divided into four domains based on Heart Rate Variability (HRV) (Hughes et al., 2019): -Temporal domain features: HRV time-domain features quantify the number of HRV observed during a given monitoring period.

text.text: In our case, 30, 60, and 120 seconds are considered.
-Frequential domain features: we applied a fast Fourier transform to separate HRV into High Frequencies (HF) and Low Frequencies (LF) components or very HF (VHF) and Very (VLF), respectively.
We used a 120 seconds window for those features. -Non-linear features: we applied Poincare Plots to extract those features.

The 1156 Wilcoxon tests indicate a significant difference in 523 comparisons. 373 are differences between the Stroop task and other steps: 129 with the Baseline, 122 with the Relaxation, 122 with the Endline, 41 from ET, 36 from ECG, and 296 from EDA features.

The remaining are 65 differences between the Baseline and Relaxation, with 13 from ET, 6 from the ECG, and 46 from EDA features, 33 between Baseline and Endline with 10 from ET, 8 from ECG, and 15 from EDA features; 52 differences between features.
Those results indicate that the Stroop task triggered the most physiological variations with 71.32% compared to other steps according to the Post-Hoc tests.
Specific features would not return to baseline during the Relaxation and the Endline steps.
But, the 5 minutes Relaxation step already reduces the previous steps' impact on physiological variations.

The 10 features that would still be impacted during the Endline (after all steps) compared to the Baseline based on the largest effect sizes are HR60s, HR10s, HR6s, HRV_HFn for ECG; ALSC, Mean_rPeak, DR_RecoveryTime_T30, Std_RecoveryTime_T30, DR_RiseTime_T120, Max_RiseTime_T60 for EDA.
Hence, this also implies that 49.61% of previously varying features (between Baseline and Stroop) came back equivalent to the Baseline during the Relaxation.
During the Endline step, 74% of features were back equivalent to Baseline.

Still, the ECG features were less represented here, probably because participants were instructed to breathe calmly to relax, which impacted their heart behavior, so it would be equivalent to Baseline.

Overall, based on r scores, subjective Stress has a perfect negative association with the Scores and a perfect positive association with the Mean response time.
Hence, participants performed worse when reporting Stress.
Subjective Cognitive load has a strong association with Score and Mean response time.
Cybersickness and sub-VRSQ visual fatigue and Disorientation have weak to moderate associations with Score and Mean response time.
Participants performed worse with state induction.
We first tested all physiological features to visualize which sensor had the most correlations with each subjective state, and the results are displayed in supplementary materials (file 17).

Overall, the average correlations between the subjective state and the physiological features are strong.
Secondly, we tested only features sorted in section 3.1.3.1 with a statistically significant difference between experimental conditions.
The Spearman tests correlations between physiological features and subjective state are displayed in supplementary materials (file 18).
Cognitive load has a perfect positive association positively with the minimum recovery time T120 and T60 (Std, DR) and strong positive associations with Pupil diameter-based features.
Stress is associated with those same features but with lower correlations.
Visual fatigue has a strong inverse correlation with HRV-derived features and fixation duration and strong positive associations with Blink and Fixation frequencies.
Disorientation and general Cybersickness have similar correlations, with a perfect positive association with Blink frequency and a strong negative association with HRV_HTI_60.
Overall, pupil diameter seems more related to subjective cognitive load but is closely followed by Stress.
The difference in correlations between Cognitive load and Stress is mainly with HRVdomain features associated with Stress but not Cognitive load.
Surprisingly, Visual fatigue correlates strongly with HRV domain features, but more logically, it also strongly correlates with Blink and Fixation features.
We expected only ET features to have such a high correlation based on previous works.
Disorientation and the total score of the VRSQ (Cybersickness) show similar correlations with physiological features.
Those results partially support H8.

We designed and conducted two experiments using Stroop tasks to test 8 hypotheses linked to three research questions listed in sections 1.8 and 2.6.

Our purposes were to measure physiological variations linked to Cybersickness, Visual fatigue, Cognitive load, and Acute Stress but also to differentiate psychophysiological variations between those states thanks to 4 experimental conditions: Control, Dual task (to trigger high cognitive load), Stressful (to trigger acute stress), and Stereoscopy (to trigger Visual fatigue and Cybersickness): see section 2.3.
Considering confounding effects, immersion duration impacts, priming, and anchoring effects, we conducted those experiments with a between-subjects and a within-subjects design.
We also considered Baselines, Relaxation, and Endline steps in the procedure to investigate how participants' physiological variations behaved after state induction.
We discuss our results by type of recorded data.

Therefore, researchers only using a specific data set in their work can also easily envision how our results can be relevant when measuring Cybersickness, Visual fatigue, Cognitive load, or Acute Stress instead.

text.text: Questionnaires were submitted only after each Stroop task.
Our purpose was to assess if participants evaluated Stroop tasks differently depending on experimental conditions and how long they have been immersed for experiment 2.
We tested two hypotheses directly with questionnaires.
Our first hypothesis was that subjective states (VRSQ, NASA-TLX, STAI-6) differ between experimental conditions (H1).
Results from the first experiment indicate that the Dual task condition induced the most cognitive load compared to every other condition and more Disorientation compared to the stressful condition.
But, reported Stress and Cybersickness were about similar.
Hence, in a between-subject design with 26 minutes of immersion, VRISE induction in our experimental conditions lightly influenced reported states.
Hence, Cognitive load is perceived differently when a highly demanding task influences cognitive resource consumption.
This also drove participants to declare more disorientation.
However, stressful noise and stereoscopy did not influence state reporting significantly.

Results from the second experiment with statistical test scenario 1 (similar to the first experiment) show that participants reported the Dual task condition induced the most cognitive load compared to every other condition.
Hence, these results align with those obtained during the first experiment.
However, in experiment 2, the Dual task and the Stressful condition drove similar Stress reports but higher than Control and Stereoscopy conditions.
Cybersickness, Disorientation, and Visual fatigue are reported to be almost equivalent in the second experiment.
Hence, Visual fatigue and Cybersickness induction with our Stereoscopy condition did not affect participants' reporting.
H1 is consequently only partially supported.
The Dual task was perceived as cognitively challenging in experiment 1 and stressful in experiment 2.
The Dual task influenced a higher VRISE reporting and Disorientation reporting.
Our fourth hypothesis was that Subjective VRISE (VRSQ, NASA-TLX, STAI-6) depends on which running order (moment in the entire procedure) they are declared after Stroop tasks (H4).
In experiment 2, under scenario 2, Cybersickness and sub-VRSQ Disorientation and Visual fatigue reporting increase with time.
The more participants were immersed, the more they reported those VRISE.
However, Cognitive Load and Stress reporting were not impacted depending on the Stroop task order.
Under scenario 3, immersion time seems to influence Cybersickness reporting (and sub-VRSQ) but not subjective Cognitive load and Stress.
H4 is consequently only partially supported.
Participants did not seem to have mental fatigue linked with the procedure duration or stress accumulation.
But, Cybersickness, Visual fatigue, and Disorientation were time-related.
Hence, how long participants are immersed drove different reporting.

Our results align with (Gradl, Wirth, Mächtlinger, et al., 2019), which showed SSQ with a significant time effect. (Henderson et al., 2012; Souchet, Xie, et al., 2022) showed that uncontrollability induced in their protocol did not influence stress reporting, similar to our noise for Stress induction.

In summary, inducing Cybersickness, Visual fatigue, Cognitive load, and Acute Stress was not always driving participants to evaluate them differently.
Inducing Cognitive load impacted Disorientation reporting with the Dual task condition in experiment 1.
But in experiment two, the significant factor was immersion duration.
Participants reporting differentiated the Dual task condition from others in both experiments.
In experiment 2, the Dual task and the Stressful conditions were rated similarly stressful, showing that participants were aroused by a cognitively challenging task similar to high noise.
Hence, cognitive resources triggering should be carefully monitored when assessing Cybersickness as it could confound Disorientation reporting and trigger stress response as well.
Immersion duration should be chosen, so participants are not impacted by Visual fatigue and Cybersickness, although it didn't seem to impact Cognitive load and Stress reporting.

Our second hypothesis was that Stroop task performances differ between experimental conditions (H2).
In experiment 1, the Dual task globally leads to lower Stroop task performance than other experimental conditions.
In experiment 2, under scenario 1, the Dual task and the Stressful conditions impacted performances more than the Control and Stereoscopy conditions.
Our correlation between questionnaires and behavioral data in experiment 1 also supports this.
While in experiment 2, all states were associated with a drop in performance, with a stronger one under Stress.
Hence, displaying stereoscopy did not impact Stroop task performances significantly compared to other conditions despite correlation results with the VRSQ (and sub-part of the questionnaire).
H2 is consequently only partially supported.
Highdemanding cognitive resources were the most impactful with the Dual task conditions in the two experiments.
Stress induction via noise slightly impacted the experiment's performance but was not different from Control and Stereoscopy conditions.
Our fifth hypothesis was that Stroop task performances differ between the running order they fulfil (H5).

Based on our results with experiments 2's scenarios 2 and 3, the order in which experimental conditions were performed and whether tasks were fulfilled at the beginning or the end of the procedure did not impact Stroop's performances differently.
This is also supported by the weaker associations between questionnaires and behavioral data determined with correlation tests compared to scenario 1.
Hence, H5 is not supported.
Cognitive fatigue, stress accumulation, and increasing Visual fatigue and Cybersickness with time did not impact Stroop task performances.
Our results contradict some previous work showing the impact of Acute stress on Stroop performances (Henderson et al., 2012; Parsons & Courtney, 2018).

Our third hypothesis was that physiological responses differ between experimental conditions (H3).
In experiment 1, 92.43% of ET, ECG, and EDA features did not differentiate VRISE from our experimental conditions.
Most features vary differently with ET features, and the Stereoscopy drives most differences with more fixations and smaller pupils' sizes than other conditions.

In experiment 2 (scenario 1), 71.19% of ECG and EDA features could not discriminate between Cybersickness, Visual fatigue, Cognitive load, and Acute Stress differentiation (eye tracker data were not exploitable).
Most features vary differently with features extracted from the EDA, and the Dual drives different physiological variations compared to other conditions 70.21% of the time.
Physiological variations between the Dual and the Stressful conditions are mostly similar.
Consequently, H3 is only weakly but partially supported as some physiological variations show that state induction drove slightly different physiological effects.

None of the previous work using the Stroop task (see section 0) attempted to differentiate physiological variations between Cybersickness, Visual fatigue, Cognitive load, and Acute Stress except one (Souchet, Xie, et al., 2022).

One explanation for the lack of comparable results with previous work is that they usually compared Cybersickness, Visual fatigue, Cognitive load, and Acute Stress induction with their baseline or a rest period only.

Despite Cognitive load and Acute stress physiological markers characterization being more advanced than Cybersickness and Visual fatigue, very few work directly try to differentiate psychophysiological variations attributable to each.

The bigger picture with our experimental conditions is that most features did not differ.
Nonetheless, we identified several features that could be a candidate for differentiation.
In other words, features that can characterize physiological variations are mostly due to one of the tested states, which come to say they should be prioritized to assess it.
In Summary, we isolated the 10 physiological features with differences between states with the largest effect sizes and how they variate (whether they increase or decrease when compared) in
Table A.13 for experiment 1 and in the supplementary materials for experiment 2.
However, Cognitive load and Stress in both experiments were mainly indistinguishable.
Although we identified features allowing us to differentiate states, most didn't vary differently.
In experiment 1, Pupil diameter is lower with Visual fatigue than with Cognitive load and Acute Stress.
Fixation duration is higher, and Fixation frequency is lower with Cognitive load and Stress compared to Visual fatigue.
Heart Rate and Heart Rate Variability are higher with Cognitive load than with Acute stress and Visual fatigue / Cybersickness.

The Standard deviation of recovery time of the mean skin conductance level of the last 120 seconds and the Arc length of the skin conductance level are higher with Cognitive load compared to Visual fatigue and Acute Stress.

In experiment 2, most mean skin conductance level-based features and HRV features variations are higher with Cognitive load compared to Acute stress and Visual fatigue and higher with Acute stress compared to Visual fatigue.
Since ET data were not exploitable, we can only hypothesize that their features could follow experiment 1's trends.
Hence, with those features, we can distinguish Cybersickness, Visual fatigue, Cognitive load, and Acute Stress in VR, but most effect sizes show that those differences are tight.

Hence, the magnitude of physiological variations differs depending if this is linked to Cybersickness, Visual fatigue, Cognitive load, and Acute Stress showing how complex it is to isolate them from one another.
Especially acknowledging that most physiological variations are similar when assessed with ET, ECG, and EDA.

Researchers specifically focusing on cognitive inhibition via the Stroop task, we recommend avoiding stereoscopy to prevent artifacts in their data collection to assess Cognitive load and Acute stress.

Our sixth hypothesis was that physiological responses differ between steps implying Baseline, Stroop, Relaxation, and Endline drive different physiological effects and that Relaxation or Endline is sufficient for participants' physiological markers to return to Baseline after states' induction (H6).
In experiment 1, the Stroop task triggered the most physiological variations, with 71.32% compared to other steps.
During the Endline step, 74% of features were back equivalent to Baseline.
The 5 minutes Relaxation step already reduces half of the Stroop task's impact on physiological variations.
However, part of the ET, ECG, and EDA domain features was not back to the Baseline at the end of the entire procedure.
In experiment 2, the Stroop task triggered the most physiological variations, with 85.40% compared to other steps.
Similar to experiment 1, features mainly returned to the Baseline during the Relaxation steps.
However, this return to baseline was lower during the last relaxation step.
Furthermore, like in experiment 1, some features were not back to the Baseline at the end of the entire procedure.

Considering that other features came back to the Baseline during the Relaxation steps or Endline, the others still impacted by stimuli were the Saccade ratio, Blink frequency, Blink duration, and Pupil size for ET, Heart rate for ECG, Rise time of the mean skin conductance level, the Arc length of the skin conductance level for EDA.
Consequently, H6 is partially supported as physiological responses differ between steps.
Still, Relaxation or Endline is sufficient for participants' physiological markers to return to the Baseline after state induction except for the previously listed ones.
Most previous works compare steps in a protocol (a given stimulus to a Baseline or a rest period) rather than states.
Ours allowed us to also compare HR for ECG, the Rise time of the mean skin conductance level, and the Arc length of the skin conductance level still being impacted by stimuli administration.
These results align with the 69 previous work on Cybersickness, Visual fatigue, Cognitive load, and Acute Stress in the Appendices section.

Our results are in line with previous works using Stroop tasks that show HR or SCL-domain features increasing with Cognitive load and Acute stress (Gradl, Wirth, Richer, et al., 2019; Ishaque et al., 2020; Kerous et al., 2020; Kalantari et al., 2021; Souchet, Xie, et al., 2022).

text.text: Our seventh hypothesis was that physiological responses differ between Stroop tasks depending on which order they are performed (H7).
In scenario 2 from experiment 2, 38.14% of features varied according to Stroop tasks running order.
Within the significant differences, 68.41% are between the first and the other Stroops, 15.13% between the second and the two following Stroops, and 16.48% between the two last Stroops.
Most features varying differently are extracted from the EDA between the first and the last Stroop.
Under scenario 3, only 6.04% of features varied whether Stroop tasks were performed at the beginning or the end.
Hence, there is a slight gap between 5-32 minutes and 33-74 minutes.
But there is a 64-69 minutes immersion threshold.
Those results indicate a partial time-related physiological variation.

Consequently, H7 is partially supported as physiological responses differ between Stroop tasks depending on how long participants are immersed, driving different physiological effects independently of specific state induction.
Our results align with previous work regarding Cybersickness and its time-related factor (Kourtesis et al., 2019; Eftekharifar et al., 2021; S. Chen & Weng, 2022).

Our results also help characterize VRISE physiological markers.
Furthermore, it shows that even very low VRISE inducers already impact physiological response.
The direct implication for psychophysiological data gathering is that peers should acknowledge that more than 1 hour of immersion might create noise in their data collection.
Our eighth hypothesis was that Behavioral and Physiological features strongly correlate with each subjective state (H8).
During experiment 1, participants performed lower with state induction, and correlations with behavioral data were stronger with subjective Stress and Cognitive load induction.
The EDA features have the most correlations with subjective states.
The difference in correlations between Cognitive load and Stress is mainly with HRV domain features associated with Stress but not Cognitive load.
Unexpectedly, Visual fatigue correlates strongly with HRV domain features.
Visual fatigue strongly correlates with Blink and Fixation features.
Hence, we can differentiate how each physiological variation is associated with each state through correlations.
In experiment 1, those variations are more associated with Acute stress and Cognitive load than VRISE with ECG and EDA features, but this is the inverse for ET features.
For experiment 2, Stroop performances were mainly associated with experimental conditions rather than in which order participants performed the Stroop task.
The correlations are similar between subjective Cognitive load and Stress under Scenario 1.
Despite statistically significant differences, the association between subjective reporting and physiological variations doesn't allow clear differentiation between the two.
Under scenario 2, subjective Visual Fatigue, Disorientation, and Cybersickness have similar associations with physiological features.
EDA features are not related to time for Cognitive load but are for Stress and VRISE.
Consequently, H8 is partially supported because behavioral and physiological features strongly correlate with each subjective state.
Their variations are linked differently with the specific state as those correlations differ depending on state induction.
Most previous work only tested differences between features and only 9 out of the 69 papers we reviewed (see Appendices) tested correlations.

text.text: In summary, correlations show that Cognitive load and Acute stress strongly affected Stroop task performances, but VRISE had weak effects.

Physiological features were differently associated with each state as ET was more associated with VRISE, although the longer participants were immersed, the more EDA features were associated with VRISE.

EDA and ECG features had some strong associations with Cognitive load and Stress, which are almost always similar to those two states showing how hard it is to differentiate them based on correlations between subjective reporting and behavioral and physiological data.
Our general hypothesis was that we can differentiate Cybersickness, Visual fatigue, Cognitive load, and Acute Stress psychophysiological variations (Hgeneral).

text.text: This paper documented an attempt to distinguish Cybersickness, Visual fatigue, Cognitive load, and Acute Stress in VR with two experiments using a Stroop task.
The use of physiological markers to assess those states suffers two main shortcomings.
First, previous work usually focus on one state at a time, making them missing alternative explanations for observed physiological variations.
Second, previous work do not consider confounding between those states.
We focused on that complexity in physiological variation interpretation (Sirois & Brisson, 2014; Argyle et al., 2021; Becker et al., 2022; Souchet, Lourdeaux, et al., 2022).
text.formatted: We focused on that complexity in physiological variation interpretation <ref type="bibr" target="#b275">(Sirois & Brisson, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Argyle et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Becker et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Souchet, Lourdeaux, et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: But we also analyzed subjective and behavioral data, often used to assess Cybersickness, Visual fatigue, Cognitive load, and Acute Stress.

We tested 8 hypotheses to give insights into three research questions. 7 out of those 8 hypotheses were partially supported as all tests on data would not appear statistically significant or with strong correlations.
The first research question was: what are the physiological features characterizing each state (RQ1)?

Previous work we reviewed would mainly indicate physiological features or indicators are similar no matter the state, and physiological variations are alike for Pupil diameter, blink frequency, fixations, HR, HRV, and SCR-derivated features.
Our results align with previous work as those features differ between the conditions where we induced states compared to the Control.
Although, our Stressful had very few differences from the Control condition in our two experiments.

In our experiments, despite relaxation steps and Endlines, Saccade ratio, Blink frequency, Blink duration and Pupil size for ET, Heart rate for ECG, Rise time of the mean skin conductance level, the Arc length of the skin conductance level for EDA were still not back equivalent baseline.
Hence those physiological features can help target Cybersickness, Visual fatigue, Cognitive load, and Acute Stress in VR.
The second research question was: Can we differentiate different states according to psychophysiological responses (RQ2)?
Previous work wouldn't focus directly on that except for notable work on Cognitive load and Stress  Alsuraykh et al., 2018a Alsuraykh et al., , 2019;; Gioia et al., 2021; Becker et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Previous work wouldn't focus directly on that except for notable work on Cognitive load and Stress  <ref type="bibr">Alsuraykh et al., 2018a</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Alsuraykh et al., , 2019;;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b102">Gioia et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Becker et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Most previous work testing covariation between states to underline their links, or when trying to discriminate each state, they would focus on subjective and behavioral data.
Our results show that it is possible to distinguish Cognitive load and Acute stress from Visual fatigue / Cybersickness, with ET, features varying more with the latest.
Although hard to distinguish, Cognitive load differs from Acute stress based on the Heart rate feature from the ECG sensor.
Cognitive load provoked more response with EDA features than Visual fatigue / Cybersickness with the ALSC feature.
However, most of those differences have very small effect sizes (this might be due to our stimuli varying only slightly from one experimental condition to another).
Furthermore, most of the extracted features from ET, ECG, and EDA showed no differences between Cybersickness, Visual fatigue, Cognitive load, and Acute Stress in VR.
Hence, the short answer to this research question is yes, we can differentiate psychophysiological responses between states.
But only with a few features, and those differences have low magnitudes.
Therefore, measured physiological responses can be very ambiguous to interpret in VR, especially with tasks triggering high Cognitive load and Acute stress such as the Stroop.
The third question was: does using VR to study cognitive load and stress trigger confounding effects in physiological measures due to Cybersickness and Visual fatigue (RQ3)?
Previous work evoke this possibility in their discussions as a limitation to data interpretation.
Our results show a threshold of about 1 hour where features vary more significantly because of immersion duration than experimental conditions.
Furthermore, results in experiment 1 with the ET feature show that pupil size, blinks, and saccades are more impacted by stereoscopy (visual fatigue provoked by accommodation-vergence conflict).
Our results also show that questionnaires partly fail to measure differences between states, while behavioral data allow limited differentiation.
For instance, Disorientation was estimated higher by subjects while the high cognitive load was induced in experiment 1.
Hence, the short answer to this question is yes; using VR to study cognitive load and stress triggers confounding effects in physiological measures due to Cybersickness and Visual fatigue.
Furthermore, suppose subjects are asked to estimate side effects, stress, or high cognitive load at rest, during relaxation, and then during/after stimuli administration.
In that case, they will likely overestimate subjective states because of anchoring and priming effects.
For future work, we encourage other researchers to replicate our procedure to contribute to standard stimuli-based Cybersickness, Visual fatigue, Cognitive load, and Acute Stress measurements.
Precisely, reproducing a within-subject study would be interesting mainly because our ET data were unusable.
Our studies took place in France.
Hence it would be interesting to investigate if results can variate depending on psycholinguistic factors.
Furthermore, our study mainly falls into the biases of including young, highly educated people with little ethnic diversity.
Hence testing the procedure with specific populations (older, less educated, less techno-enthusiast, and considering various ethnicities) remains necessary.

"states" means Cybersickness, Visual fatigue, Cognitive load, and Acute Stress: -H1: Subjective state (VRSQ, NASA-TLX, STAI-6) differ between experimental conditions implying states are differently perceived depending on state induction -H2: Stroop task performances differ between experimental conditions implying states have different influences on it -H3: Physiological responses differ between experimental conditions implying the 4 Stroop task -hence states inductionstimuli drive different physiological effects -H4: Subjective states (VRSQ, NASA-TLX, STAI-6) depending on which running order (moment in the entire procedure) they are declared after Stroop tasks implying how long participants are immersed drives different reporting -H5: Stroop task performances differ between the running order they fulfill, implying time influences them -H6: Physiological responses differ between steps implying Baseline, Stroop, Relaxation, and Endline drive different physiological effects and that Relaxation or Endline is sufficient for participants' physiological markers to come back to Baseline after state induction -H7: Physiological responses differ between Stroop tasks depending on which order they are performed, implying how long participants are immersed drives different physiological effects independently of specific state induction -H8: Behavioral and physiological features are strongly correlated with each subjective state showing that their variations are linked differently with specific states The general hypothesis is Hgeneral: we can differentiate Cybersickness, Visual fatigue, Cognitive load, and Acute Stress psychophysiological variations in VR.

We only have results allowing for partial hypothesis support, showing that Cybersickness, Visual fatigue, Cognitive load, and Acute Stress differentiation are difficult.
But, it has direct relevance for several research fields.

First, cognitive psychology increasingly using VR should be aware that Cybersickness and Visual fatigue can be an artifact of their physiological measures of Cognitive load and Acute Stress, especially if they aim at using ET features.
Second, even acknowledging the influence of those side effects on measures, part of physiological variations can be wrongly associated with only one state.
I.e., literature increasingly points to confounding between Cognitive load and Acute stress, but Visual fatigue and Cybersickness can also confound obtained measures.
Our results support this with an about 60 minutes immersion "limit."
Thirdly, with our stimuli and setup, EDA features allowed the most states differentiation.
However, ET was more sensitive to Visual fatigue / Cybersickness compared to Cognitive load and Acute Stress and ECG to Cognitive load compared to Acute Stress.
Fourthly, the study design influenced physiological variations as more differences were observed during the withinsubject (experiment 2) than the between-subject study (experiment 1).
The results from this article can be considered by peers using VR to study Stress and Cognitive load.
They can now estimate how Visual fatigue and Cybersickness could impact psychophysiological variations even with standard stimuli such as the Stroop task.

Conversely, peers focusing on assessing, detecting, predicting, and reducing Visual fatigue and Cybersickness can consider those results to explain part of the measured variance in their studies with ET, ECG, and EDA.
In summary, Stress, Cognitive load, Visual fatigue, and Cybersickness can confound one another, which implies noticeable limitations in interpreting psychophysiological measurements in VR.
Consequently, studies using physiological sensors should be parsimonious with their claims.
Studies focusing on Acute stress and Cognitive load should assess VRISE through questionnaires to consider alternative explanations.
Nevertheless, we observed with our experiments that questionnaires are very limited, and subjects tend to overestimate VRISE when facing complicated tasks.
